name: Waymo Safety page: an operator's overview of autonomous driving safety
title: Waymo Safety page: an operator's overview of autonomous driving safety
answer: Waymo's Safety page is a corporate landing page about the company's safety program for fully autonomous driving technology. It states that Waymo was born as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served its first fully autonomous rides in 2015. Its most useful point is that Waymo supports the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy by advancing Safer Vehicles and Safer Speeds through research and deployment of its autonomous ride-hailing service. The supplied text does not include methodology or crash rate comparisons.

sections.body: Waymo publishes this page at waymo.com/safety. It is a corporate safety landing page rather than a report, study or data release. Its scope is Waymo's safety program for fully autonomous driving technology, its company history and its alignment with road safety campaigns. The text does not state a publication date. It says Waymo was born as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served the first of many fully autonomous rides in 2015. The page is written by the operator itself and has a promotional tone.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says Waymo is as rigorous and innovative in its safety practices as it is with its technology. It says the company has built a comprehensive safety program to guide its testing and development of fully autonomous driving technology. Waymo states that it believes the status quo of road safety is unacceptable and that autonomous driving technology can save lives and improve mobility for all. It gives two historical markers, that Waymo was born as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and that it served the first of many fully autonomous rides in 2015. The page then describes the Vision Zero Network as a collaborative campaign to help communities reach their goals of Vision Zero, which it defines as eliminating all traffic fatalities and severe injuries while increasing safe, healthy, equitable mobility for all. It describes the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy as a critical step toward an ambitious long-term goal of reaching zero traffic fatalities on American roads. Waymo says it supports the National Roadway Safety Strategy by advancing Safer Vehicles and Safer Speeds through the research and deployment of its fully autonomous ride-hailing service, Waymo. The supplied text repeats the opening statement and does not provide safety performance data, methodology or crash rate comparisons.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives two dates, 2009, when Waymo says it was born as the Google Self-Driving Car Project, and 2015, when it says it served the first of many fully autonomous rides. It defines Vision Zero as eliminating all traffic fatalities and severe injuries while increasing safe, healthy, equitable mobility for all. It says the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy has a long-term goal of zero traffic fatalities on American roads. It says Waymo supports that strategy by advancing Safer Vehicles and Safer Speeds. The supplied text gives no crash rates, no mileage figures, no methodology and no comparisons with human drivers.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in transportation can use this page to see how an autonomous vehicle operator publicly frames safety. It connects fully autonomous driving to the Vision Zero goal of eliminating traffic fatalities and severe injuries and to the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy. It also shows the company positioning its autonomous ride-hailing service as a way to advance Safer Vehicles and Safer Speeds. Because the supplied text is a landing page, it is useful as a statement of intent and policy alignment rather than as evidence of safety performance. A reader looking for methodology or crash rate comparisons will not find them in this harvested text.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: This is a commercial operator's landing page, not an independent study or a detailed safety report. The supplied text does not include methodology, crash rates, mileage, disengagement data, comparisons with human drivers, regulatory filings or third party verification. It does not state a publication date. It covers only Waymo's own program and does not discuss other autonomous vehicle companies or other transportation modes. The page is promotional in tone and repeats its opening statement. It does not substantiate the claim that Waymo publishes a complete safety record, because the harvested text contains no record beyond general statements and two dates.
